1:
The false balance is read as a mechanism, as a date and as a word. Adam Clarke takes the instrument apart: one end of the beam is longer than the other, so that it turns sooner at one end; and the just weight is the perfect stone, weights having first been made of stone. Charles Ellicott reads the repetition as evidence, since the same proverb and two more in praise of true weights stand elsewhere in the book, which suggests the cheating grew common as the commerce of the nation developed; and adds that it is useless to raise the superstructure of a religious life without first laying the foundation of honesty. Keil and Delitzsch work on the terms, making abomination a participial noun in which the act of abhorring is transferred to the thing done. Matthew Henry makes honest dealing a test of religion, since he is not an honest man who is not devout, and catches the excuse: men think there is no sin in that by which money is to be got, and while it passes undiscovered a blot is no blot till it is hit. John Gill puts it the other way round: there may be common honesty without the grace of God, but no grace of God without honesty.

On pride and shame Clarke turns psychologist. The proud man thinks much more of himself than anyone else can, and expecting treatment according to that worth, which he seldom meets, is repeatedly mortified; the humble man looks for nothing but justice and can be disappointed only by praise, which he neither expects nor desires. Gill answers with a list of instances, the angels that sinned, Adam and Eve, Haman and Nebuchadnezzar, and at the end of it the fall of Rome Papal. Henry adds that pride is a strange sin in a creature who springs out of the earth and lives upon alms. Ellicott gives one line, that they lack the grace of God to keep them from falling; John Wesley glosses the balance as all false weights and measures in commerce.

The integrity that guides is where the commentary turns technical. Keil and Delitzsch spend their space on the opposed word, rejecting two Arabic derivations, to step out and to turn about, as improbable and a third, to smear, as scarcely admissible, and setting against them three Jewish authorities who gloss the word as wavering, falsifying and misrepresentation. Ellicott takes the same word in the sense of covering a matter up, and says such men pervert the truth until they can hardly distinguish right from wrong. Henry makes the principle do the work: a man whose principles are fixed has a plain way, and need not tack about every time the wind turns. Gill puts three guides in order, the Spirit first, then the word as a lamp to the feet, then the sincerity of the heart.

The day of wrath sorts them by horizon. Keil and Delitzsch define it as the day when wrath breaks through the limits of long-suffering, as the prophets use it. Henry brings it nearer, since the day of death is itself a messenger of wrath, and riches will neither put by the stroke nor ease the pain, much less take out the sting. Clarke concedes that among men riches can do all things, but cannot purchase the remission of sins. Gill applies the wrath to Rome Pagan and Rome Papal. Ellicott distinguishes the days, since riches profit in no day when God visits his people, much less in the day. On the smoothed way Keil and Delitzsch are careful that the word means evenness of surface, not straightness of line; Ellicott makes it progressive, the just man receiving more light and seeing more clearly how to avoid what besets him, while the wicked darkens his conscience until he stumbles as in the night and falls.
6:
The hope that dies with the wicked man is treated four ways. Adam Clarke notes the irony that hope was not made for the wicked and yet they most abound in it: they hope to be saved with their face toward perdition, but their hope goes no farther than the grave. Matthew Henry gives it an image, the hypocrite wrapping himself in his hope as the spider in her web, then divides the loss: the worldling leaves the world he expected to continue in, and the hypocrite comes short of the world he expected to remove to. John Gill counts what perishes, the expectation of longer life, of riches, honour and pleasure, and adds that the expectations others had of him perish too. Keil and Delitzsch describe the man rather than the hope, one to whom possessions and pleasure and honour are the highest good and who rocks himself in measureless hopes; and they record an ancient version that turns the clause round, so that it is the righteous man whose hope does not perish at death.

Where the wicked comes in the righteous man’s stead, Henry answers with history: the gallows, the den and the prison were prepared for three men who escaped them while their persecutors came in their place, and the sea that opened for one nation drowned the other. Charles Ellicott allows two senses, that misfortunes pass by the righteous and fall on the wicked, or that the righteous is taken away from the evil to come while the wicked lives on to suffer in his place. Clarke keeps to sudden calamity, where God rescues one and leaves the other, so that justice does its own work because mercy has been rejected. Keil and Delitzsch alone enter the objection: experiences of the opposite kind are not wanting, since divine justice shows itself here only as a prelude, though as a rule destruction falls on the godless.

The word rendered hypocrite divides them further. Clarke says it would be better translated infidel: the hypocrite pretends to religion for secular purposes, while the infidel disbelieves revelation, lives in pollution, and is zealous in propagating his notions. Ellicott glosses it the profane. Keil and Delitzsch report that three old translators rendered it hypocrite, its later sense, but that in ancient Hebrew it means the man resolved upon evil; and they refuse to alter the text against two scholars who would, since it stood as it is before every other translator. Henry stays with the flattering tongue, than which no tongue is more fatal, and holds that knowledge of the devices of Satan delivers the just, seducers not being able to deceive the elect. Gill applies it to false teachers and their heresies, and John Wesley puts the deliverance in five words, from the infection of the hypocrite’s evil counsel.

On the rejoicing city the readings run from the political to the ecclesiastical. Keil and Delitzsch take the city for the state, report a conjecture that such proverbs may be older than the days of Asa, and note that an ancient version omits parts of both verses, combining the halves that remain. Henry is shrewd about the general feeling: even those with no great stock of religion have a good word for a good man, while the wicked may have well-wishers among those altogether such as themselves but get ill-will from everyone else. Clarke makes the good man a blessing by his example, his advice and his prayers. Ellicott takes the blessing of the upright to be chiefly their prayers, offered for the people they live among as they were of old for a doomed city and in the captivity. Wesley balances the clauses, sincere prayers and wholesome counsels against curses, oaths and blasphemies. Gill alone dates the fulfilments, in the days of Constantine when persecution ceased and at the reformation when the pure doctrines of the Gospel were revived.
12:
Contempt of a neighbour is defined before it is condemned. Keil and Delitzsch say the phrase covers degrading a man in a derisive or insulting manner, and that neither German nor English has an expression that quite covers it; the intelligent man keeps his judgment to himself, knowing he is not infallible and not acquainted with the heart. John Gill supplies the motives: a man despises his neighbour because he thinks himself wiser, or is richer, or fancies himself holier, like the Pharisee; or else the word means he wants a heart, that is, grace. Adam Clarke draws the contrast in practice, the fool bringing his neighbour’s defects into the most prominent view, the prudent man hiding what he can and putting the most charitable construction on the rest. Matthew Henry makes silence an act of friendship, and observes that a man undervalues himself when he undervalues one made of the same mould; John Wesley reduces the second clause to bearing reproaches patiently.

On the talebearer two reach for the same trade. Gill says the word signifies a walking merchant, who takes up his wares in one place and vends them in another, and that two versions render it accuser, the name given to the devil. Clarke calls him the walking busybody, the trader in scandal, and adds that such men will tell even their own secrets rather than have nothing to say. Keil and Delitzsch derive the word from going hither and thither, and settle a dispute over which half of the verse carries the subject. Henry alone adds a limit to the duty of concealment: the faithful man will not disclose what he is trusted with unless the honour of God and the real good of society require it.

The proverb on counsellors is where the commentary turns on a criticism. Keil and Delitzsch quote a scholar who mocks the maxim, saying that those who have longest resorted to many counsellors have learned that too many cooks spoil the broth and that he who asks long errs; they answer that ecclesiastical and political affairs illustrate the clause more fully than ever. Henry keeps to the practical case: two eyes see more than one, and if our advisers agree our way is the clearer, while if they differ we hear what is said on all sides. Gill makes the leaderless people a ship without pilot or helm; Charles Ellicott disposes of the verse in a line about having plenty to guide the state.

Suretyship produces the one place where a commentator quotes another by name: Gill reports Henry’s observation that Christ became surety for us when we were strangers and smarted for it, but knew our circumstances beforehand and was not broken by the payment. Henry argues from stewardship, that we may not use our estates as we will, and that a man must be just to his family or he is not true to his trust. Ellicott corrects the rendering, reading for another rather than for a stranger, and in quiet rather than is sure. At the gracious woman the versions intrude. Keil and Delitzsch report an ancient translator who read a different word and added a whole line, that a woman who hates the right is a throne of dishonour. Clarke quotes the same expanded text: a good wife is an honour to her husband and a bad wife his reproach, so how careful a man should be whom he marries. Henry sets the clauses side by side, the gracious woman as solicitous for her reputation as strong men are for their estates, and as honourable as a valiant man. On the merciful man Keil and Delitzsch reject the reading of many interpreters who reverse subject and predicate, since the man who denies himself nothing is an egoist and no benevolent man. Clarke reports the saying that such a man frets his flesh off his bones.
18:
The deceitful work deceives in two directions. Matthew Henry makes it self-deception, the sinner building on sand and promising himself by his sin what it will never give, so that it cuts his throat while it smiles on him. Adam Clarke puts it in a line, that nothing the wicked man does is durable except his crimes. Charles Ellicott agrees that the work ends in nothing, and re-renders the second half: the sower of righteousness works a sure reward for himself. Keil and Delitzsch report the versions instead: a Latin translator makes the second half independent, as though a different word stood there, and two eastern versions read it as though fidelity were the reward, though as the text stands one verb governs both halves. At the next verse they set aside more renderings, since a Greek version read a righteous son for genuine righteousness, and the word cannot mean holding fast, as two moderns would have it, but means upright and genuine. Clarke turns physician: godliness promotes health, while wicked men live not out half their days.

The joined hands are read four ways. Keil and Delitzsch report a Greek rendering about putting hand in hand unjustly, taken by one commentator not of a man who can be bribed but of a violent one. Ellicott offers two senses, from one generation to another, or, most probably, the hand upon it, that is, assuredly. John Gill reports a Jewish commentator who reads it from hand to hand, the reward of their work passing from the hand of God into theirs. Clarke alone goes abroad for the gesture, citing a traveller who reports that the Hindoos sometimes ratify an engagement by laying one right hand on another. Henry keeps to the confederacy: numbers and unanimity in sin will not protect the sinners, and it will not excuse a man to say that he did as his company did, witness the flood brought on a whole world of ungodly men. John Wesley reads the fortification as a numerous kindred and issue.

The jewel in the snout draws the fullest comment in the chapter, every voice adding something. Keil and Delitzsch note that this is the first emblematic proverb in the book, where the two lines stand as figure and import, and the ornament is the nose-ring, hung from the right nostril over the mouth, in use since the patriarchs. Ellicott gives the same detail, adding that it is worn in the East still. Gill takes the figure from the other end: swine are ringed with iron to stop them rooting, so a gold ring is unbecoming and soon carried to the mire. Clarke quotes an old English version in its original spelling and notes that the nose jewel is common in Asiatic countries. Henry allows that beauty is itself a jewel of gold where there is grace to guard it, quoting a Latin line that virtue is the more graceful for coming from a fair body, and then laments the waste as ill-bestowed and quite misplaced. Wesley answers with eight lines of verse addressed to the woman herself, bidding her set her charms out and show the jewel in her snout.

The last proverb turns on a word. Keil and Delitzsch reject the usual reading, that the expectation of the godless is the wrath of God, and take the word in its other sense of want of moderation, so that their hope is presumption. Ellicott takes it the same way: they do not ask in the way or for the things God wills, so that expecting their desires fulfilled is presumption. Henry keeps the wrath, the wicked desiring the woeful day so that judgments may remove those who stand in their way and they may fish in troubled waters. Gill keeps to the first clause, that good is what the righteous man continually desires and what he has here and hereafter.
24:
The paradox of scattering and increasing is illustrated, not argued. Matthew Henry supplies the figure the verse omits, that what is given increases as corn increases by being sown, and works out the other half: a man may grow poor by meanly sparing, by not paying just debts, by not providing what is convenient for his family and not allowing the expense that would preserve his goods, which cramps his industry and destroys his credit. Charles Ellicott answers with an old epitaph: what we spent we had, what we saved we lost, what we gave we have. John Gill notes that four versions add the words his own, and applies the whole to the man who disperses the truths of the Gospel and is enriched by spreading them.

On the soul of blessing they converge. Gill insists that the blessing soul does not merely pray for the poor and give them good words but bestows good things liberally. Keil and Delitzsch derive the word for blessing from the idea of spreading out, so that to bless is to cause increase by word and deed, and observe that the blessing which goes out from such a soul comes back to itself. Adam Clarke states the return most strongly: the man who distributes in the right spirit gets more good than the poor man who receives the bounty, and the wonder is that God gives the property, gives the heart to use it aright, and recompenses the deed, though all the fruit came from himself. Henry has God returning it in dews and plentiful showers till there is not room to receive it.

The corn-hoarder is condemned by all of them and defended in passing by one. Keil and Delitzsch identify him as the corn-usurer a prophet describes, holding back his stores in scarcity because he speculates on a higher price. Henry turns it into a rule for men with stocks of corn, that they sell at the market price, be content with moderate profit and not aim to make a gain of the judgments of God, and calls it a noble charity to help keep the markets low. Clarke adds a second curse, that of God, lying as a canker in the man’s money in this life and in his soul throughout eternity. Gill reads the withheld corn as the withheld Gospel, naming the forbidding of ministers to preach and the locking up of the Scriptures in a language the people do not understand. Ellicott alone grants the other side, that the truth of the proverb is not affected by the fact that the dealer’s selfishness benefits the community in the long run, since the rise in price limits consumption.

The closing proverbs are handled briefly. Keil and Delitzsch set out three synonyms for seeking, from roots meaning to cleave, to try, and to be early abroad. Gill and Henry both take that last sense, Gill of the man who in the morning of his youth inquires after the best things, Henry of the man who rises early to what is good and procures the love of all about him; and Henry adds that seeking mischief is set against seeking good, since those not doing good are doing hurt. On the trust in riches Keil and Delitzsch see two trees behind the verse, one withered and one whose leaf is always green. Henry makes the riches a broken reed which not only disappoints the man who leans on it but runs into his hand and pierces him. Gill has him falling as leaves fall in autumn; Ellicott gives the reason in a line, that riches are uncertain and prevent a man trusting in the living God. John Wesley glosses the section in half-lines: to scatter is to give liberally, to be made fat is to be enriched with temporal and spiritual blessings, and to sell is to sell upon reasonable terms.
29:
Who troubles his own house is not agreed. Keil and Delitzsch canvass the versions before deciding: one eastern version renders the clause twice, of deceit and of the opposite of avarice, and a Greek version makes him a man who behaves towards his own without affability, but the parallels point rather to a niggard, and the same verb is used of the prophet blamed for a drought. Charles Ellicott agrees in a line, taking the trouble to be avarice. John Gill will not choose among the causes: bitterness to a wife, provoking children to wrath, menacing servants, idleness that fails to provide, a worldly spirit that hurries business beyond measure, a mean temper that withholds food and clothing, or plain profuseness. Matthew Henry reduces the list to two extremes and condemns both: an extreme earnestness in pursuit of the world, with fretfulness about losses and niggardliness at home, to which he adds the man who keeps up feuds in his family to serve his own turn; and a want of common prudence in the man who neither minds his business nor goes about it well, and so becomes servant to the wise in heart.

The wind they inherit is glossed three ways, each an image. Henry says what such men get will be not only empty as the wind but noisy and troublesome with it. Adam Clarke makes the man who dissipates his property by riotous living as unsatisfied as one who feeds upon air. John Wesley makes him as unable to keep what he gets as to hold the wind in his hand.

At the tree of life the question is what the fruit means. Keil and Delitzsch reject the Greek, which makes a tree of life grow out of the fruit of righteousness and so reverses the relation of fruit and tree; the fruit is not the good a man’s conduct brings him but his activity itself, which is a tree of life for others, since his words and actions quicken and refresh them. Ellicott says the same in fewer words, that the righteous brings life and healing to his neighbours and the wise man attracts them to himself. Henry goes a step further: the righteous are trees of life, and the wise are trees of knowledge, not the forbidden knowledge but the commanded; and recalls that the proselytes of the patriarch were called the souls he had gotten. Clarke keeps the Hebrew plural, the tree of lives, which increases the bodily and mental vigour of those who eat of it. Gill turns it round: the fruit is what grows on Christ and is received from him.

The last verse carries its own mark. Henry observes that this is the only one of these proverbs with a Behold prefixed, which intimates not merely an evident truth but an eminent one; and he allows two ways of taking it, either of punishment throughout, so that if the righteous are chastised the wicked will fare worse, or of reward to the one and punishment to the other. He then admits what the proverb does not say, that many sins go unpunished and many services unrewarded, which itself argues a judgment to come. Keil and Delitzsch explain the construction as an argument from the less to the greater, and note that the verb has two faces, denoting full requital of either kind. Gill gives both senses and prefers the harder, that the recompense is the chastisement of the righteous, which they have only here, since in another world there is no sin to chastise. Clarke and Ellicott both leave the Hebrew for the Greek, which reads that if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear, and note that an apostle quotes it word for word; Ellicott adds three names of righteous men who were punished. Wesley settles it in two words, punished for his sins.
